14.0.s.en: (1) Joab's plan to bring Absalom back

14.0.0.en: The king's heart was toward Absalom: always thinking of him and longing for him.

14.0.1.en: Joab was close to David and well informed about his affairs, and he sought to bring Absalom back for the following reasons:

14.0.2.en: 1- Because he knew how much David loved Absalom and longed to see him.

14.0.3.en: 2- He expected that Absalom must surely return, so he wanted to win the love of David and Absalom by being the intermediary in his return.

14.0.4.en: 3- He knew how much the people loved Absalom, so he expected that he would become king after his father; but his being far from the people of God could stir doubt among the people whether they would choose Absalom or his elder brother Adonijah.

14.0.5.en: 4- Joab knew of David's anger against him for killing Abner, so by bringing back Absalom, the killer of his brother, and David's pardoning him, David would forgive Joab and he would win David's love.

14.1.0.en: Tekoah: a village south of Jerusalem about 20 km from it. The ruins of the same name are found in its place to this day.

14.1.1.en: In the village of “Tekoah” there was a woman renowned for wisdom and sound reasoning in speech and in presenting matters, so Joab sent for her to charge her with a task, and he asked her to pretend grief, wearing mourning clothes and not anointing herself with perfumes, so that she would appear as a woman grieving for a dead person dear to her.

14.2.0.en: Put the words in her mouth: he taught her what she would say to the king.

14.2.1.en: He asked her to seek to appear before the king and speak to him with the words he had taught her.

14.3.0.en: Help, O king: crying to the king for help in some matter.

14.3.1.en: The woman went in to the king and bowed down before him, crying to him to help her face a problem that tormented her and kept her sleepless.

14.4.0.en: The king asked her the reason for her deep grief, and she told him an imaginary story, as Joab had instructed her, to use as a parable that applied to David and his two sons Amnon and Absalom.

14.4.1.en: The story began by saying that she was a widow whose husband had died and left her two sons, who quarreled while working in the field where there was no one to part them, and the quarrel developed into a struggle with the hands, and one struck the other and killed him.

14.5.0.en: The men of the Law judged the killer of his brother to death, according to what the Law decrees, and asked the mother to hand over her son the killer so that the sentence of the Law might be carried out on him. The woman went on to present the matter, saying that if she did so and handed over her other son to be killed, they would thereby quench the light of her life, meaning her remaining son, the killer, who was the only son left to her; and her husband's name would be blotted out from the earth, for he would have no descendants left with the death of both sons, and her husband's inheritance would pass to others of the sons of the clan.

14.6.0.en: The woman skillfully used her power of reasoning and persuasion, so that David was moved by her words and felt her problem, and he reassured her and asked her to be calm, saying he would issue instructions to the men of her clan to pardon her son the killer in consideration of her circumstances.

14.7.0.en: The woman realized that King David's exempting her son involved a breaking of the divine commandment (the Law), so she called down upon herself that she should bear the guilt of transgressing the commandment and that David and his throne should be guiltless of this offense. She based this on the Law, which allows the pardoning of a killer in some circumstances out of mercy (Deut 19:4, 5).

14.8.0.en: David assured her of his protection of her from anyone who confronted her and insisted on handing over her son, and told her to bring him to the king, and he would command him not to molest her.

14.9.0.en: The revenger of blood: the nearest relative who demands the blood of the slain.

14.9.1.en: There shall not one hair of thy son fall to the earth: no one shall touch him with harm.

14.9.2.en: The woman asked him to confirm his promise to her with an oath so that this promise would be made firm and the members of her clan would cease to demand that she hand over her son, lest the revenger of blood add to the calamity of the killing of one of the two sons the new calamity of killing the remaining son, and her pain and weariness be doubled and her misery increased.

14.9.3.en: David wanted to set her heart completely at rest, so he granted her request and swore to her by the living God that no one would be able to harm her other son in any way or touch him with harm.

14.9.4.en: May you use wisdom in your speech with others to persuade them and win them and call them to carry out the mercy you desire or any good work, and not use commands or rebuke, which are rejected most of the time.

14.10.0.en: Here the story that was taken as a parable of David's position toward Absalom came to an end, with the woman obtaining the required promise from which there is no going back, namely the pardon of the killer. So she decided to prepare to enter into the real subject, and she asked the king to permit her to continue speaking so as to disclose to him a certain thing, and he permitted her.

14.10.1.en: Whoever has authority over others should be patient in listening to their cases, allowing them to explain the details of their complaint, and listen to them with all deliberation and attention, so that his judgment in the end may be fair.

14.11.0.en: The woman began to make use of the king's pardon of her son (in her invented story), saying to him that if he had pardoned her son out of mercy for his mother, why had he not taken account of the wish of his people to justify another person in a similar matter (she meant that the majority of the people of Israel loved Absalom and justified his killing of his brother). And why did he insist on keeping the killer son (she meant Absalom) in exile, although what applied to my son, and your oath that you would not allow anyone to harm him, applies also to your son? Your insistence on not forgiving him makes you guilty before God, because you swore that no one would harm my son, and this is your son, so how can you not forgive him?! And because David was a wise man, he could understand the wisdom of this woman who spoke in a parable.

14.12.0.en: The wise woman gives the king here a profitable sermon: that all must die and return to the earth like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again; so if you are grieved over Amnon, death is the destiny of every living person.

14.12.1.en: God Himself devises means, gives graces, and works in the heart and mind of the offender so that he returns to Him and He pardons his offense, so that he does not remain far from God's care). By these words the woman means that if God does this with all mercy toward the sinner, and this is His dealing with erring human beings, then all the more should David pardon his son and call him back from his exile and restore him to himself. The woman took advantage of her knowledge that the people loved Absalom and that David himself loved him and longed for his return (ch. 13:39), but feared that he would be unjust in forgiving the killer.

14.13.0.en: I have come to you, O king, and presented to you this matter of pardoning Absalom, although the people were frightening me, saying that the king would not listen to my entreaties; yet I dared to come and gave the example of the mother and her two sons, so that perhaps you might be convinced by my mediation and pardon your son.

14.14.0.en: In the end the woman summarizes her story, by which she means it to be a parable calling David to forgive Absalom, and she says to him: all my hope is that you listen to me and do me justice against the revenger of blood who seeks to kill my other son and to remove my name and my son's name from the people of God and from the inheritance of the holy land that He gave to His people. All this moved David to forgive Absalom.

14.15.0.en: May the final decision of my lord the king concerning the pardoning of his son Absalom be another comfort to me, as your first word was about the killer of his brother in the field. You have pardoned my son because you saw that it was good, and you are the best at discerning between good and evil because you are sent by God to serve His people; so may your judgment in the case of Absalom also be for the good of your people, and may the Lord support you and bless your steps.

14.16.0.en: The king understood the hints the woman was making, which applied to him and his son Absalom, and that her aim in the end was that the king should review his position toward his son Absalom. He also understood that there must be a planning mind behind this woman, moving all of this, so he asked her not to conceal a matter about which he would ask her, and the woman showed her readiness to answer what he would ask.

14.16.1.en: And we note David's readiness to bring Absalom back because he loved him, although the story the woman told did not apply entirely to Absalom, for he was, for example, not an only son but had many brothers... but David longed to see his son.

14.17.0.en: The king concluded that Joab, who was the person best informed about the king's circumstances and his longing for Absalom (v. 1), was the one who had urged her to what she did and said, so he asked her whether it was Joab who had prompted her in what she said, and the woman answered with an oath that what the king had concluded was correct, and she confirmed to him that Joab was indeed the one who had charged her with what she said.

14.18.0.en: None can turn to the right hand or to the left from ought that my lord the king hath spoken: without addition, omission or distortion.

14.18.1.en: To fetch about this form of speech: so as not to approach the subject directly.

14.18.2.en: The woman added that Joab did not wish to confront him himself directly with the words, so he charged her with the matter. Then she praised the intelligence and discernment of the king, who concluded from the story she had invented that he was the one meant by it, concerning his position toward Absalom, and that by this wisdom of his he was like the wisdom of the angels, to whom the Lord gives the grace of knowing many things that human beings do not know.

14.18.3.en: This woman, by her wisdom and good words, was able to win David and he agreed to her request; so may you use the right time and praise others and offer them good words founded on prayers, that God may give you wisdom in winning them, and you will be at peace with those around you.

14.19.s.en: (2) David permits Joab to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem

14.19.0.en: I have found grace in thy sight: I have found acceptance of my person from you by your honoring me.

14.19.1.en: The king was convinced that he must change his position toward Absalom, which in fact he longed to do inwardly, so he summoned Joab, who was the true intermediary between him and his son, and asked him to bring his son to Jerusalem.

14.20.0.en: Joab rejoiced because the king accepted his mediation, so he bowed down before him in expression of his thanks, repeating the statement that the king's acceptance of his mediation showed his great trust in him, and that this was an honor to his person in which he took pride.

14.21.0.en: Joab went to Geshur to bring Absalom in fulfillment of the king's order, and took him with him back to Jerusalem.

14.22.0.en: Absalom returned to Jerusalem, the capital of King David, but the king decided to deprive his son of seeing him, as a proof to the people that he was still displeased at what Absalom had done before in killing his brother Amnon, and also as a message to Absalom that he was still displeased at his killing his brother Amnon, so that he would humble himself and repent.

14.23.0.en: Absalom was beautiful and more handsome than all the sons of his people, and he was praised and extolled by all the people, for his whole body was marked by beauty.

14.24.0.en: After the king's weight: units of weight equal to 8 grams.

14.24.1.en: Hair was a sign of Absalom's handsomeness, so besides the perfumes with which he anointed it, he cared for it with all care, and out of his great admiration for it he cut it only once a year, being compelled to, because it was very thick and made a weight on his head. He used to boast of it and weigh it, and its weight reached about 1.5 kilograms, especially since it was anointed with oils and perfumes, and he even put gold filings on it so that it would shine, as a kind of luxury and display.

14.25.0.en: Absalom had three sons and one daughter, whom he named after his aunt Tamar, and she was beautiful like her father, her aunt and her grandfather David (1 Sam 16:12).

14.25.1.en: Absalom was preoccupied with his beauty, so he departed from purity of heart and life with God, and his end was regrettable, as we shall see in the following chapters. So do not be preoccupied with your beauty, your position or your possessions, for they are all passing and will distract you from the salvation of your soul, so that you depart from God and fall into many sins. And if God has given you something, thank Him for it.

14.26.s.en: (3) Absalom's attempt to see the king

14.26.0.en: After Absalom's return from Geshur he did not meet his father even once for two whole years. His deprivation of meeting his father for two years, in addition to the long period he spent in Geshur, which was three years, affected his psychology and was reflected in his behavior toward his father, as will come in the next chapter. He did not benefit from this long period in repentance and humility, but his heart was filled with pride, jealousy and envy, and he sought to take the kingdom from his father, as will appear in the next chapter.

14.27.0.en: Absalom was distressed by the long deprivation of meeting his father and of being received in the royal palace as one of his sons, so he thought of turning to Joab to mediate for him in his request to see his father. But Joab refused to mediate this time, and despite Absalom's pressing, Joab continued to refuse and did not go to Absalom; perhaps he knew that David would probably refuse for the sake of justice and so that the people would not stumble, and Joab did not wish to embarrass himself.

14.28.0.en: Absalom resorted to a trick so that Joab would come to him, and he ordered his men to burn the barley crop in Joab's field next to his own, in order to provoke Joab so that he would come to him protesting the burning of his field, and Absalom's men carried out this order.

14.29.0.en: His trick succeeded, for Joab was angry at the burning of his field and went to Absalom, asking and raging why he had burned his field!

14.30.0.en: Absalom justified his deed by saying that it was his trick to provoke him to come to him, since he had refused to come to him more than once, and he wanted to send a message by him to the king asking him the reason for permitting him to return to Jerusalem without permitting him to meet him; it would have been better to leave him in Geshur with his grandfather than to be in Jerusalem deprived of seeing his father. He charged Joab to ask the king to permit him to see him, and if the king still considered him guilty of anything, to let him kill him, for that was better for him than to continue in this situation. By this Absalom showed his love and longing for David, to stir his father's feelings toward him, relying on his compassion and fatherhood, although Absalom was evil and did not love his father, as will appear later.

14.31.0.en: Joab conveyed Absalom's wish to the king, and the king's heart softened toward his son and he agreed to permit him to see him. So Absalom came to his father and bowed down before him in a bow of respect and reverence, and the king rose from his seat and embraced his son with intense longing and kissed him.

14.31.1.en: How beautiful was David's fatherhood and forgiveness. May we have pity on sinners that God may have mercy on us, and perhaps by our pity we may draw them to repentance.
